title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
hook: Licenses are supposed to travel with AI datasets and models — but across 232,270 supply-chain paths, obligation-bearing licenses survive end-to-end under 7% of the time.
key_points: Traces 232,270 dataset→model→application chains across Hugging Face and GitHub to see whether license obligations survive redistribution.
Two forms of 'license laundering': unlicensed artifacts gaining definitive labels downstream, and one license category being swapped for another.
62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license — concentrated in a few foundational datasets.
Every obligation-bearing license category has under 7% end-to-end survival, while permissive licenses survive 95.1% of the time.
Upshot: the license on a downstream model or app often can't be trusted to reflect its real upstream obligations.
content_html: Every dataset, model, and application in the AI ecosystem carries a license, and its obligations are supposed to propagate as the artifact is reused and redistributed. This paper is the first to measure whether they actually do.
extra_html:
Tracing the chain

The authors follow 232,270 dataset→model→application chains spanning Hugging Face (datasets and models) and GitHub (applications). They quantify two forms of "license laundering": when an artifact with no declared license acquires a definitive label further downstream, and when one declared license category is replaced by another during redistribution.

Obligations wash out

The results are stark. 62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license — concentrated in a small set of foundational datasets. Every obligation-bearing license category falls below 7% end-to-end survival, while the permissive category reaches 95.1%. In other words, restrictive terms mostly disappear as artifacts move downstream, and the license attached to a final model or app is a poor guide to its real upstream obligations. The paper closes with recommendations for practitioners, model publishers, rights holders, and platform owners. Jewitt, Li, Rajbahadur, Adams, and Hassan, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Linear Ensembles Wash Away Watermarks
related.hook: Text watermarks survive paraphrasing — but not arithmetic. Averaging the outputs of 3–5 different models cancels the signal almost entirely, and improves quality while doing it.

related.title: AI Watermark Evidence Fails Forensic Readiness
related.hook: Laws like the EU AI Act and California's SB 942 assume watermark detection can hold up in court. Tested against forensic and legal admissibility standards, three leading methods collapse.

related.title: The Pile: 800GB of Diverse Text
related.hook: Web text alone leaves gaps. The Pile stitches together 22 curated sources — academic and professional — so a language model picks up knowledge plain web crawls miss.

related.title: LAION-5B: Open Image-Text at Scale
related.hook: CLIP and DALL-E showed huge, noisy image-text data is gold. LAION-5B made that public — billions of CLIP-filtered pairs anyone can train open models on.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'license laundering' in an AI supply chain?
flashcards.back_html: When license obligations fail to propagate through redistribution — e.g., an unlicensed artifact acquires a definitive license downstream, or one license category is silently swapped for another.

flashcards.prompt: How often do obligation-bearing licenses survive end-to-end across the studied chains?
flashcards.explanation_html: Every obligation-bearing license category fell below 7% end-to-end survival, while permissive licenses reached 95.1% — obligations mostly wash out downstream.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't you trust the license shown on a downstream AI model or app?
flashcards.back_html: Obligations rarely survive the dataset→model→app chain — 62.3% of chains pass through an unlicensed artifact, and permissive labels dominate downstream regardless of upstream terms.
